name: Foolproof Pan Pizza
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt sets out to recreate the thick, fried-bottomed, focaccia-like pan pizza of childhood Pizza Hut memory, and frames the recipe around removing the three things that make home pizza hard: kneading, stretching and transferring. He uses a no-knead dough because flour's own enzymes cut the proteins into shorter pieces overnight while yeast gas jostles them into a gluten network at least as strong as a kneaded dough, with better flavor, provided hydration stays high, around 65 percent. The stretching problem disappears because a wet, oil-coated ball slides out to fill a greased cast iron skillet or cake pan on its own over a couple of hours, needing only fingertip docking to kill the big bubbles that would otherwise balloon and shed their toppings. Building the pie in the pan removes the peel and stone entirely. He pushes the oven to its maximum, 550F, because fast bubble expansion gives both a crunchier exterior and a more open crumb, and he finishes with grated hard cheese after baking.
comment_digest: The fix cooks report most often is for a pale, soft bottom: after baking, set the hot pan over a burner on medium or low for a few minutes to crisp the base without overcooking the top, which several say rescued the pie. Ovens topping out at 500F work but need longer, with reports of 18 to 25 minutes, and one cook using a 10-inch pan with only a 7.3-inch cooking surface still got a wet, pale crust at 25 minutes. Pan size is flexible: the full dough works in a single 12-inch skillet, and one cook made 1.5x split between a 12-inch skillet and a 9x13. Active dry yeast substitutes for instant at about 1.25 teaspoons, and pre-shredded part-skim mozzarella works despite the note calling for dry aged. One reader challenges the 400 g to 2.5 cups flour conversion. Others find the dough too soft to ball neatly and simply drop it in the pan.
